The New Jersey Question þÿ The hull ot the American House of Representatives is yet a hear garden, and the administration members elect continue to act like a congregationof miscellaneous jacobins. It is well and truly remarked bv a correspondent of the Courier vestorduy morning, that " no faction in the national convention of ('banco, during the fiercest fury of the revolution, ever made bolder strides to retain power wrongfully, than is now making bv a portion ol the friends of the administration." The facts in the case of the \7ew Jersey election, which has been made the pretext, for all this uproar and confusion, lie in a nut-shell ! and there is not a man, woman or child in this nation, who, with proper understanding a of the facts, would hesitate to bestow the most unequivocal language of condemnation upon the factious conduct of the administration m mb'rsof Congress in this matter. þÿ The facts, substantial! v. am tb se. At the Congressional election of New Jersev, iri October of last year, there was a concerted ell >rt hv the partisans of the national administration to carry in the destructive candidates, at. any and every hazard, no matter how illegal or dishonorable the means. þÿ Frauds, gross and monstrous, were committed wherever there wis rascality enough on the one iiaiid, and negligence enough on the other, to allow of them In the towns of Millville and South Ainhov, the frauds were so obvious, as well as outrageous, and the elections in those towns were so illegally con-

ducted, that the county returning oilieers set them entirely aside. Had the votes of those towns all been counted, five of the administration candidates would have been elected, and one of the Whigs Had the polls of those towns been purged of the illegal votes, arid all the legal votes been counted, the entire Whig delegation would have been elected. Hut, for gross illegality and fraud, the returns of the entire towns were set aside by the county canvassers. The laws of Y'vV Jersey direct the county clerks to carry the respective county returns to lite Governor, w ho, with his Privy Council, is required to c ist up the whole returns so received, and on ascertaining which of the candidates have received majorities of the votes, the Governor is directed to furnish the the said candi Int' s with their certificates of election, under the broad seal of the .Slate. þÿ The Governor and Privy Council have no right, by law to look behind the returns received Irom the proper returning oliicers of the counties. The duty of the Governor and his I'riw Council end with the canvass ol the county returns as received ; and the certificate of the Governor, under the seal of the State, form- the only legal and constitutional evidence of member ship upon which a member can take his seat. Without such certificate, tin memb-'r can lawfully take a seat. þÿ And with such certificate, no member was ever before denied Ins scat But it suited not the jacobins, in and out of Congress, to allow the observance ot the law.

A clamor was early raised in New Jersey against the course pursued by the Governor and his Council. It was insisted that they ought to have gone behind the returns as made to Ihoui, and to have counted the voles

of Millville and South Arnboy þÿ illegal as well as legal. But in no event had the Governor a right to do any such thing. Had fie been convinced, even, that every vote cast in tltose towns was a legal one, and that the elections had been in other respects legally conducted, he still could not have gone beyond itie returns furnished by the county returning oliicers. The clamor upon the subject, however, was so great, that the Whig members who had received their certificates, notwithstanding tiie fact that by a subsequent legislative investigation the imputed frauds had been tuily established, proposed to test the confidence, and tfie sincerity, of the destructives, by a frank and manly oiler to bring the question again before the people. W ith tiiis view, they offered to resign, if the destructive candidates would also resign their pretended claims, and appeal to the people by a new election. But no : These dear friends oi the people had not faith enough for that. They had faith, however, elsewhere, if not in the people. They felt that if fraud could not triumph in New Jersey, it could prevail some where else ; and they have not been mistaken. By tampering with a recreant Secretary of the Privy Council, who is also Secretary ot the State, the rejected candidates possessed themselves ol the returns of the i!iogaily-held elections of Millville and Smith Amboy, authenticated by the seal of the said recreant Secretary, and armed with a certificate furnished by him, illegal in itself, eutitely

unknown to the Iqw, by an officer who had 110 more right to interfere in the matter than a Chinese hoppo, these modest gentlemen present themselves at the door of Congress þÿ nay they rusii impudently into the hull þÿ claiming to be the true representatives of the very people whose own decision of the controversy they had shrunk from inviting ! Such is a just and true history of this eitraordinary ease, down to the day appointed lor the assembling of Congress. With its subsequent history our readers are pretty well acquainted although not quite as well þÿ as we could have desired, for we have not been able to quote as largely from the stiring debates that have occurred as we meant to do. Several of the speeches of the legally returned members from New Jersey we have been constrained to omit, as also the lucid and very able argument of Air Barnard, of Albany þÿ decidedly the ablest of the session, thus far. Still, the public has seen that the action of the foul plot against the Whigs of New Jersey was in due season transferred from that state to Washington, and that the clerk of the last House of Representatives, whose duty, by custom, it was to call the roll of members, and assist in the organization of the House, by effecting an election of Speaker, was ' nothing loth" to play a part in the conspiracy. In the first place, without color of law, usage or precedent, he decided to consider the illegal and spurious certificate of the clerk of New Jersey to lie of equal force and vir-

tue w ith iIk legal document, under the sign manual of the Governor, and the great seal of the state. And in the second place, while calling the roil of members, he volunteered to announce that the seats of five of the New Jersey members were contested þÿ a fact which lie had no right at that stage of proceeding to know, officially, or in any way to take cognizance of þÿ and having made the annunciation, he committed the farther of-

3J3t1373R3&3IT&SS &T33% fence of deciding against the regular certified members from New Jersey, by ajjecttng not to decide the question at all. From that hour to the present, all has been disorder and wild confusion in the House ot Representatives. Parliamentary law mid and precedent have alike been outraged, the code of even common decency tram; led under foot. The entire uniform practice of Congress, in its organization, and upon too subject of contested elections, from .be foundation of the government, is disregarded ; :md with impudence, brazen and unblushing, vj destructive members who were in the last two Congresses, turn their backs upon thc.r own votes and speeches, without aped'- v r justification, and laugh at their inconsistency, as though it were a good political joke þÿ Were the quotation not hackuied, we should be disposed to exclaim with the poet þÿ 1 I he re not some clioseti curse þÿ Some hidden thunder in ihe stores of Heaven Red wmIi urcomrnori wrath, to blast an administration, and the partizans who sustain it, which depends upon such means for its support 1 There is not the color of justification for the course pursued on this occasion by the destructive members of the House, and the clerk who so shamefully violated his duty by becoming their instrument. There is no doubt, that the members bearing the certificate of tiie Governor of New Jersey were the members chosen by the legal votes of the people. But no matter whether they were so or not. They had the only evidence

of membership known to the laws þÿ either to the laws of the House, or to the laws of the state of New Jersey þÿ and it was the duty of the clerk of the House to call their names, and no member had a belter right than they to vote upon any and every question, u'ttil their scats, if contested, should have been given to others, after an investigation by the standing committee of elections, and in the due course of the practice ol the House.

Amusements of War. þÿ When Louis XIV. besieged Lille, the Count de Biouni, governor ot the place, was so polite as to send a supply of ice every morning for the king's dessert. Louis said one day to the gentleman who brought it, " I am much obliged to M. de Brouai for his ice, but 1 wish he would send it in larger portions." The Spaniard answered without hesitation. " Sire, he thinks the siege will lie long, and he is afraid the ice may be exhausted." When the messenger was going, the Duke -de Charrost, captain of the guards, called out, " Tell Brouai not to follow the example of the governor of Douai, who yielded like a rascal." The king turned round, laughing, and said, " Charrost, are you rnad !" " How, sir I" answered he " Brouai is my cousin." In the lYIemoires de Grammont, you vvill find similar examples of the amusements of war. You remember that when Philip of Maccdon vanquished the Athenians, in a pitched battle, they scut next morning to demand their baggage ; the king laughed, and ordered it to lie returned, saying, " I do believe the Athenians think we did not fight in earnest"

TRADE WITH CHINA. Advices were received late on Saturday afternoon bv the government from China to the 29th of May. Captain Elliot left Canton on the 21th, and arrived at Macao on the 27th, together vvitli ail the persons who had been detained as hostages. Orders had been given by the Chinese authorities for the expulsion of Mr. Dent, four gentlemen connected with the firm of Jardine, Mathcson. and Co., and of Mr. Junes, all connected with the opium transactions. It was understood that all the opium which had been given up to the Chinese was to be sent to þÿl ekin, there to be disposed of as his Celestial Majesty might best think fit. We extract the following from a private letter: þÿ The trade is entirely stopped, and all the merchants arc about to leave Canton. The 10 hostages detained have been released, but are never to enter Canton again. No trade can he carried on until the intentions of the British government are known þÿhere. þÿ Twenty thousand two hundred and ninety one chosis of opium, the v alue of which is 3,000,000/ sterling, have been delivered up to the Chinese. All British subjects will be out of Canton next week. Every ship is to day out of the reach. T he Chinese opened

Every man interested in the security of our Indian empire must view the present position of our affairs with no small share of anxiety Very late accounts lrom the eastward indicate that a war with Burmali is inevitable. The King has marched three considerable armies towards our frontier, and in other respects Ins conduct has been ol a character to leave us no alternative but to break with him. It is probable that after t he rains the Madras government will be called upon to furnish the necessary force for this service, to act in Conjunction w ith the fleet under Admiral Maitland. The experience gained in the last war w ill give us a great advantage in this, and the result is in no respect doubtful In liujpootana m titers aie in a very unsatisfactory state. Colonel Sutherland, the resident, has called upon Government for a large force to subjugate at once and effectually these turbulent states, and next cold season this allair will he settled. The troops stationed at Nusserbad and Neemuch will suffice for tins service The Punja ul> is hkolv to become the scene of civil st rife. No sooner did the death of tin; old Maharajah reach the Sikh army destined against Canid, than the whole broke up and scampered oti, leaving Col. Slade with a few followers stockaded at the mouth of the Kvliar Pass. So much for the value of the Sikh alliance. The voting king, llurruk Singh, however, show's some vigour, and hitherto, has succeeded in preventing any thing like an out-

break. This, however, is certain, that for some time the Punjaub must be a source of great anxiety to the Indian government : and not of anxiety only, but of expense, as a large force must be maintained on the frontiei to be ready for every contingency. In Nepaul we also require to he on the watch, the people being greatly disallected towatds us. and only waiting a favoiable opportunity to stiike a blow. But it is not from our ancient connections alone that we have to fear annoyance at present; the Ameers of Sinde have been detected in holding correspondence with Dost Mobamcd ; and as they arc a treacherous and most profligate race, and their territory enables them to control the navigation of the Indus, government, there is every reason to believe, has determined completely to put them down ; indeed, it is much to he regretted that Sir John Keane had not done this en passant The news from the army is not very important. According to one account, the whole force, with the exception of a Bengal regiment of native infantry left to garrison Candahar, was to march on Cubnl about the 17th of June. Another account is, that the Commander iu Chief had received advices of a large Persian force being on the march against Herat, and if this were placed beyond all doubt, a portion of our troops would certainly he dispatched for ll.e protection of that place. Provisions had been collected with great difficulty, stud it was still doubtful whether it would be possible to place the army on lull rations.
The Chinese and Persian questions remain in statu quo. They, too, may fie regarded among the number of our present embarrassincuts, tho' more properly questions lot home

decision. But they act injuriosh upon our domestic broils, as giving disaffected parties grounds for talking, and ii"t very respectfully, of on r power, w hich fats been made to appear contemptible in both cases. An experiment was tried earlv on Tuesday last with a newlv invented projectile, intended expressly to meet and set at defiance the improvements suggested bv the various French commissions, for the navv, and which have attracted a greater degree m public attention in England, from their avowed object being " to the advantage ol the power which had the fewest great ships of the line, and the largest population; and conseiju-ntly to the advantage of Frame over L.n vlanil þÿ þÿ The recent report by Mr. Jnullrv evinces the same jealousy and the same object. A large and strong built boat was the subject of the experiment ; the distance was left to choice, with the single proviso, that the object tired at should be in sight. The invention for Captain Warner, launched with his own hand the destructive mis- le which, reaching the boat at the water line, exploded, fairly heaving her up, and scattering the planks into shivers. One plank alone of the whole retained a breadth of about three inches, and perhaps two feet in length; the rest( and the keel itself, as they fell after the lapse of some seconds into the water, presented a mere mass of floating splinters to the eye, and portions of the wood were carried into the neighbouring fields to a considerable distance. The whole destruction was effected by the agency of two and a half pounds of combustible matter projected by an instrument of perhaps ten or a do/.en pounds weight. þÿ There was no recoil whatever, nor any smoke

or noise till the shell itself exploded against the vessel, and then the percussion of ail was tremendous, as it threw down the nearest spectator, and was felt at a still greater distance like the discharge of an eight pounder at least. At Kingston it created great commotion, as the explosion was attributed to the pinvilr mills at Hounslow; and, since the tact has become known, the excitement has greatly increased.

v ht,. HA-; «-.;r'rv . - '& No vessel of the line probably could have resisted a shock, or escaped total destruction from even the small quantity of combustibles experimented with. Napoleon and his brother in law left the carriage, which drew up to one side, and. ns the rain fell in torrents, they sheltered themselves under the porch of a church. Happiness is much more equally divided than some of us imagine. One man shall possess most of the materials, hut little of the thing ; another may possess much of the the thing, but very few of the materials. In this particular view of it, happiness has been beautifully compared to the manna in the desert, ho that gathered little had no luck ; therefore, to diminish envy, let us not consider what others possess, but what they enjoy ; mere riches may he the gift of lucky accident or blind chance, but happiness must he the result of prudent preference and rational design ; the highest happiness then can have no other foundation than the deepest wisdom ; and the happiest fool, is only as happy as he knows how to he.

4 <|( MMUI New York Gazette, October 7. Most Destructive Conflagration. Scarcely have we scanned ihe accounts of the lire in Philadelphia, before we aie culled upon to record a calami ty of our own, compared vviih which the disaster of our sister city dwindles into a very ordinary occurrence. The angel of destruction has again been upon us, again brandished his red bezom over our dwellings, and " walked in blazing majesty" through our streets. From seven o'clock on Saturday evening, to broad day light yesterday, the city scarcely ceased for a moment to hear the solemn fire hell, or to see the red flames of conflagration casting their glare over almost every point of the oily þÿ and not only from the city but from Long Island and New Jersey ; for while four extensive fires were doing their work of destruction at as many points in New York, Brooklyn and Jersey City, sent upward their blazing columns of fire. The supply of water had became very much exhausted by the previous drains upon the reservoir during the night, &. the hydrants yielded so scantily that the Third Ward Hose Company which was promptly on the spot, found its efforts paralvzed. The United States Hotel was in the greatest danger, but the spirited exertions of the inmates of that establishment, by keeping the roof and dome covered with wet blankets, preserved the building. These elibrts were aided by the forcing engine belonging to the house, or it would probably have shared the fate of the building next to it, which was destroyed. Bv half past 3 o'clock, nearly the entire

square between Front, Fulton, and Water streets, and Burling Slip þÿ thirty-two buildings was one sheet of living flame, and presented a scene grand even in its gloom. .Nothing remains but a row of buildings on Fulton street, much injured, but not destroyed. The rest are but a heap of smouldering ruins. At four o'clock, the aspect was most terriffic. and there seemed no bounds to i he extent of the threatened calamity, hut fortunately a favorable change of wind took place at this time, and lines having been formed to the river, a plentiful supply of water was obtained, and the firemen took heart, The farther progress of the flames was siaid At one time it seemed almost, impossible to preserve the most valuable part of tin eiiv, down Water, Front, South, and even Pearl streets. The Tontine buildings on the corner of Wall ami Water streets, directly opposite t he office of this paper, was two or three times on fire from the cinders, though at very considerable distance from the spot ol actual conflagration. Of the aggregate amount of loss, there is, as there always is, a great dispai ity of estimate þÿ some making it a million and n half of dollars, and others putting it as low as half a million. Both the minimum and maximum we are satisfied are wrong. We have endeavored to obtain good data, and to lake the best opinions on the subject, and we rcaliy believe the amount will he found to vary little from one million of dollars.

From the Morning Courier and New York Fnquirer, December 21. SIX DAY1 LATER FROM ENGLAND. The Liverpool packet ship South America, Captain Baii.ey, was telegraphed yesterday afternoon, and in the course of the evening we received through the kind attention of Captain Bailey, the files of English papers tent us bv this conveyance. Their dates are to the 21st from London, and 22d lroin Liverpool. Judging from these, we do not think, that any material change has occurred in the slate of affairs, since our last advices. We should say the London Money Market has assumed a more healthy appearance. & that the Cotton Market at Liverpool maintained itself far better than was anticipated by the most sanguine. The inferiority in the quality of the late Wheat crop, is a prominent remark in every statement which we read, coming from the different markets in the United Kingdom American State Securities are sadly depressed, and on these " the conspiracy" has had a most baneful effect--more so, we think, than was agreeable to one of the parties to it, as it will be seen, that they have found it necessary to obtain and publish the opinion of Mr. Wkbstf.r, in regard to the legality of the debts contracted by the States. The Queen of England, it would appear certain, is to be married to her cousin, the second son of the reigning Prince of Saxe Coburg, in May next. In the political situation of that countrv no change is perceptible. The leaders in the late Chartist insurrection are prosecuted with unrelenting rigour. þÿ Much alarm had been excited in all classes

bv the temporary indisposition of the Duke of Wellington, þÿ an alarm commensurate with the eminent services he has rendered his country. The situation of Spain seems little improved, notwithstanding Don Carlos has left the scene of the conflict. Madrid was menaced with an insurrection, and troops had been summoned to the capital by the Government to overawe the population. Esmarteko has for the present given up his pursuit of Cabrera, and the Count d'Espaone. a celebrated leader of the Carlists. has been murdered. Between the Porte and Mehemet Ali, matters remain in their former position. London, Nov. 21 . We regret to learn that three commercial failures have taken place to-day ; one of the parties are connected with Lloyd's, as brokers, and one in the East India trade. There has been more disposition manifested on the part of the public to-day to make investments in the British securities, particularly the heavier annuities ; and there is no doubt that the discredit which has fallen on the United States securities, and the difficulty of realizing them in this market, will tend to turn the tide of spare or unemployed British capital towards British securities, which, under any national calamity, have never, as it were, been annihilated by a refusal to pay the dividends. This cannot be wondered at when we consider that the American paper debt cannot be much less than 81 10,000,000. London, Nov. 18th. Money þÿMarket. The quarterly averages of the weekly liabilities and assets of the Bank
of England, published in last night's Gazette, compared with the October returns, show an increase in the stock of bullion ol T 10,000,--

DAITSK ?:BSVltSNM3£ R&WKKRlXr&S AT33 The securities have diminished £1,000.000, and the deposits- £002,000, while the circulation is also £377,000 less The " rest1 is also decreased by £07,000, having sunk from £3,1 18,000 to £3,051,000. This result will produce considerable disappointment as the public were prepared to find that t lie present returns would exhibit a favorable change in the resources of the establishment, and that the influx of the precious metals in particular to their coffers, would have been considerable. When the manner, however, in which these returns are made up is considered, it will appear. that though the average stock of bullion is on I v £10,000 greater than in the October account, yet the actual quantity in hand must be much greater, because the drain continued in September and October, and it is but very lately that specie began to flow back to the Bank in any considerable quantity. Indeed, the large arrival ot the $2,500,000 by the linogene frigate is not taken into account ; and it is generally understood that the actual stock of bullion now held by the Bank of England is about £3,200,000. Still, although money is called a little easier, we see no symptoms on the part of the Bank Directors to relieve the market by adopting a more liberal course of action; and although there is every disposition in othei quarters so to do. the conduct of the Bank of England deters them. The country banks cannot prudently extend their transactions while the Bank ol England continues to contract the circulation,

and the consequences of this restrictive policy are now severely experienced in the manufacturing districts: for although the prices of raw cotton seems still to keep up, tiiose of manufactured goods have fallen very much of late, as the holders have been obliged to realize at any price, in consequence of the want of the usual assistance from the banks, ; and we hear thai soine foreign merchants in consequence are beginning to appear as buyers. This is, in one respect, a iavorable feature, as promises that things have come down to such a level as will induce the foreign merchants to send their orders; but it will be attended, in the first place, with serious loss to the present holders of goods. The bad state of money matters in America, and the unsatisfactory accounts from China, seem to have produced some influence on the English funds to-dav, although there was little done but the prices are rather worse than yesterday. THE DUKE OF WELLINGTON. From the Times of yesterday.. It is with unfeigned arid grateful rejoicing that we find ourselves authorised to remove entirely whatever alarms may have been caused by the melancholy announcement in yesterday's Times, of a dangerous attack of illness having visited the first man oi this age and nation. The language in which the intelligence was made public must have led almost every body to apprehend that something in the nature of paralvsis or apoplexy had befallen the saviour of his country We can assure our readers that there was

no shadow of foundation in such a fear. The Duke having lived rather full one day, hud starved himself the next, þÿ eating on Sunday last, as we understand, nothing trore than a crust of bread for bis dinner. The next morning, after an equal slight berenkfast, be mounted his horse, and went out lor some hours with harriers . Alter his long fast and

violent exercise, he returned home in a state of much exhaustion, and fairly, in a tainting fit dropped off his chair ; after which lie went to bed, giving positive orders that a dinner to which he had invited several military friends, should proceed as if nothing had happened. His Grace slept comfortably all Monday night, and has since been rapidly getting well. The only really distressing fact about the case is, that the duke, at the age of seventy, does not seem to have yet discovered the value of his own precious life, and generally takes no more care of himself than a boy of eighteen or twenty. London, Nov. 21. As no mystery is any longer observed with respect to the subject for which the Privy Council is summoned on Saturday, we may observe that it is in contemplation that the marriage of her Majesty shall bo celebrated in April next. Portsmouth, Nov. 18. The Pique frigate. Capt. Boxer, anchored at Spithead this afternoon, 22 days from Quebec, bringing home Sir John Colborne, who landed at Plymouth on Sunday last þÿ The Pique brings little or no news ; she has on hoard upwards of 100 military invalids, as also a few naval. The Cleopatra and Sesostris, two large steamers, arrived at Spithead on Sunday, on their way to India, commanded by officers of the East Indian navy. Both these noble vessels proceed to their destination under sail, reserving the use of the machinery until their arrival. Bombay, Oct. 7. I have little to add to the despatch 1 forwarded to you by iast packet. The war in

Cabul is concluded, and the army is now ou its return into our own territory. A force tias been left, by authority of Lord Auckland, consisting of one Queen's Kcgiuient and the rest Bengal troops, sufficient lor lire Shah's protection, and to maintain the peace ot the country, until such time as his own troops Lecunie thoroghly disciplined, and ours can be dispensed with. In forming his arn.y Seliah Souja will have the benefit of English officers and die advice and assistance of Sir A. liurucs as resident at his Court. þÿ The general ordcts of John Kcane and full particulars relating to the force, will be found in the papers of the 1st instant. Sir John Kcane will in person conduct the Bengal troops through the Kyber pass and the Punjaub, into Upper India, and threafter proceed to Simla to visit the Governor General, preparatory, as is said to his resignation of the command he holds and to his going home in December. The Bombay lorce under General Willshire returns by wav of Candahar, Shawl, and the Bolan Pass, into Upper Scinde, where it will probably winter. The guns and men sent to Herat under Major Tod, had arrived without any accident or molestation, and the work ol reparation was proceeding, though the place is described as still in a sadly dilapidated slate, and the country all around a complete w aste, just as the Persians left it. Dost Mahomed has succeeded, according to latest a< counts, in making his escape across the Hindoo Koosh, and is believed now to beat Balkh,
but many seem to think that he will come into Schah Soojah's terms after a time, when he sees that his cause is hopeless. His s n, Hydcr Blum, is still a prisoner at Gluznec.

Disturbances of a 'ery serious character have occurred among the working population ol South Waies, chiefly in the neighborhood of Newport, Monmouth. City, Saturday evening, December 7. þÿ A n expectation has prevailed in the city for some days past, that the directors of the Bank of England have had it in contemplation to reduce the rate of interest on money advanced for discount 6 to5$ percent. This notion was in some degree strengthened by the tenor ot the last notice which was issued by the directors of the Bank of England, intimating their readiness to make advances on the deposit of approved bills of exchange, not having more than six months to run, at 6 per cent interest, þÿ until further þÿnotice. It does not appear, however, that the directors, at their weekly meeting, which was held on Thursday last, come to any resolution on the subject ; at least, up to last evening, no intimation of the kind was communicated to the Stock Exchange, or to the public generally. I'he expectation, however, that such a measure as that alluded to might have been resolved upon by the directors, influenced favorably the markets lor all descriptions of

stock, whether domestic or foreign. Upon calm consideration, however, the leading capitalists of the city weie of opinion, that the directors of the Bank of England are not ycj in a sufficiently secure position to make any reduction in the value of money, or to in. crease their circulation of notes. The territory of this Duchy, though prosperous and thriving, and larger than that of Saxe-Meiningen, the native country of the Dowager Q.ueen, is still not of a very considerable extent. The Duchy of Saxe Mei ningen contains eighteen square (German) miles, and 55,000 inhabitants ; the Duchv of Saxe Coburg Saalfeld twenty seven and a half square miles, and 85,00!) inhabitants The public revenue of Saxe Mei ningen amounts to 350,001) florins, that of Saxe Coburg Saalfeld to 500,000 florins. Prince Albert is a young man, and would not succeed bis father. In establishing the Protestant faith the house ot Saxe Coburg took a prominent part, and there are only a few Catholics in the small district of Lichteiibero. the remaining population generally professing the Protestant faith. The ancestors of the Duke of Saxe Coburg Saalfeld were among the leaders of the Saxons who came over to this country, when in the 5th century the (tomans quitted Britain, which, being exposed to the incursions and devastations of the Piets and Scots, applied to Sa ,ooy for succours. Numerous brave troops were then obtained from the native country of Prince Albert, and their descendants ate found in ail ranks of the British nation. In 81!) the victorious Egbert, to whom the family of the Duke of Saxe Coburg were related, became King of the provinces, having Saxon settlements, and he then ordered that they should be called England. Nineteen years he reigned over ihis newly-established kingdom, and was fol-

lowed by a long series of Saxon kings, under whose mild sceptre this country improved and thrived so much that it was generally respected. Considering this, the reigning Duke ot Saxe Coburg Saalfeld cannot be considered a stranger in this country with whose interests his house became early connected. He is. moreover, generally esteemed in Germany, and beloved bv his subjects. Several years ago he issued a liberal Constitution, under which the inhabitants of his dominions enjoy perfect religious and political liberty. The following is a sketch of the life of his »oii. Prince Albert, born August 2(1, INI!) His earliest education the Prince received at the castle ot Ebrenburg, where eminent professors, from the College of Coburg, and other masters, daily attended. When he had completed his eleventh year, his mother, Louisa, daughter of Augustus, Duke of Saxe Gotha Altenburg, died. This caused the Duke, till ho should have contracted another marriage, to put Prince Albert under the care of his aunt her Royal Highness the Duchess of Kent. He subsequently resided for some time at Kensington and Claremont, and ot course had an opportunity of occasionally partaking of the lessons intended for Princess Victoria. Thus they became it appears, acquainted with one another in their early childhood. On Dec. 27, 1832, the Duke ol Saxe Coburg formed a second matrimonial alliance with the Princess Maria of W urtemburg, and Prince Albert then returned to Coburg, in order to resume and
finish the course of instruction which lie had begun there. When he had completed Ins 17th year he cnt<-red the University of Bonn on the Rhine, and attended lectures on the

classics, mental philosophy, history, statisties, mathematics, politics, and political economy. A uong the numerous distinguished Professors ol that celebrated seat of teaming is Augustus William Von Schlegel. Thus a most favorable opportunity presented to Prince Albert of pei fecting bimsell in English, the correct ac. cent ol which he had before acquired at Kensington and Claremont When he had li ished Ins studies at Bonn and returned to Coburg, the inhabitants of the Duchv vied with one another in demonstrations of the heartfelt inteiest they took in the prosperity of the Ducal house. Deputations were sent to the Duke to congratulate him on the consuinuration of the education of the prince ; poems were presented to Prince Albert welcoming him on his entrance into public life : and there were all over the country illuminations, balls, and dinners in commemoration of this important period in the life of Prince of Albert. In 1838 he came over witlt his lather to this country, to witness the coronation ot her Majesty. They stayed lunge r at the palace of Buckingham than all the other guests, and the Duke of Saxe Coburg Saalfeld, was particularly distinguished bv her Majesty, who, previously to Ins departure, conferred on him, with great ccremonv and in presence of a numerous attendance of Noble Lords, the Order of the Garter, On their return from London, preparations were made for a tour to Italy, and in December 1838 they set out. attended by Baron Stockmar, who lias been lor several years employ-

ed in the allairs of the Duke of Saxe Coburg and his tclutivcs. It was deemed necessary to make a short stay, at .Munich, in order to take, on several questions relating to Italv, the advice of the King of Bavaria, who had been several times in Italy. To the Bavarian capital, then, the Duke accompanied the I mice, and the most marked honours were paid to them there, the public considering the brilliant expectations of Prince Albert well founded, rumours to that effect having been generally circulated by the journals of Germany. Prince Albert afterwards passed into Italy, and on his return visited Vienna. When he entered his apartment at the Castle of Coburg, the first object which struck his eyes was the full length portrait of her Majesty, which hail been sent him as a present. It is the portrait which, by express command of her Majesty, was painted by A. E. Chalon, Esq., R A. The German papers generally call him Albrecht, which, however, is not a name different from Albert. This will best be seen from the following paragraph translated from the þÿ German þÿEncyclopedia, by Professors Etsch and Gruber þÿ Albert, or þÿAlbrecht, says this excellent work, þÿ is contracted from Adal and bed, and means of noble birth, also a landed nobleman Generally speaking, Albert was formerly more in use in Germany, and afterwards the second form, Albrecht, prevailed, still both words continue to be promiscuously þÿused. In ancient German records instead of Albert is also found Alberic ; and as ric is the English rich, the

modern German reich, in the same manner bed is also an old Saxon word, relating to the English birth and born. Adal is the modern German Adel, and in ancient German records both forms are likewise found. There occurred in history some very distinguished personages of the name of Albert. Among them is Albert I. Duke of Austria, aud afterwards Emperor of Germany.

INTENDED ROYAL MARRIAGE. The "marriage of the hereditary Grand Duke of Russia with the Princess J\Iarv of Hesse Darmstadt seems to be decided on. þÿ The following is an interesting anecdote on the subject þÿ þÿ There sprung up some years since, it is not known how, some doubt as to the birth of the Princess Mary of Hesse Darmstadt þÿ doubts which had effect even on the mind of her father, and alienated somewhat from his affections his lovely daughter, now not more than 15. Hence when the heir to the Russian throne undertook his pilgrimage in search of a wife thro' Germany, to review the young Princesses of the numerous sovereign families, the Princess of Hesse Darmstadt was omitted on his list Alter having travelled from principality to principality in search of beauty þÿ dark and fair þÿ the Hereditary Prince reached Hesse Darmstadt, pleased to repose in a court which contained, as it appeared from his list, no marriageable princess. At a court circle, after the preparations were over, the Grand Duke suddenly remnrked, in the corner of the saloon, a young lady clothed in simple white, and like a Cinderella, unnoticed. The Russian Prince inquired of the Grand Duke who she was ; and his royal highness replied with some embarrassment, that it was his daughter, the Princess Mary. The Russian Prince, struck with the beauty and simplicity of the princess, instantly went up and accosted her, and in a few hours was enamoured enough to dispatch a courier to fSt. Pelers-
burgh, to say that his choice was irrevocably þÿmade. Just Published

At the creation, God, intending to give his creatures a Sabbath, said that they were "all very þÿgood þÿ suited to his gracious designs. But part of those designs was the appointment ol a weekly day of rest; and as man's nature is adopted to a Sabbath and requires one, he is not in the situation for which his Greatoi designed him, if it be withheld. You might as well deprive him of his nightly rest as of bis weekly Sabbath ; þÿ the mischief, though mor slow, would not be less certain. boldly to keep the Sabbath, would notwithstanding be thankful for the Sunday rest, if he could prevent others taking his |t>usinoss out of his hands on that day ! With our glasses we could distinguish them at the windows watching our ship slowly beating into the harbor, and waving their handkerchiefs as signals of welcome. Our trip among the Windward Islands was delightful ; we have seen some of the loveliest scenery in the world ; the ddlerent nations and states of society we have visited have gratified our curiosity ; our ship was large and commodious, our table was spread with luxuries ; the most entire harmony and kind feeling has existed among the passengers. 1 should by all means advise invalids, who may hereafter visit St. Croix for a þÿwinter s residence, to make an excursion to some other islands. Such a voyage breaks up the monotony of West India life, is beneficial to þÿone s health, and presents a great variety of novel and interesting scenes. But no place in the \\ esl Indies can be compared to St. Croix, as a residence lor the invalid. Here arc concentrated advantages which are found no vvliercelstj. The roads are excellent. In Barbadoesthe roads are tolerably good. In most of tfie

islands the highways are miserably had, and would deprive the invalid almost entirely of that essential lequisite to health, abundant and pleasant exercise. InSt Croix, the roads are perfect; smooth and hard for the carriage ; the weakest invalid may drive over them without experiencing a jolt; the sick may drive over plains ; the lovers of the picturesque over hills. From St. Croix there is constant communi cation with New York. At other islands vessels sail irregularly to and from the United States. Tiie vessels which do sail furnish very inferior accommodations on the voyage ; the invalid must therefore sutler much on the passage ; and during the winter must often, and for weeks together, feel a painful anxiety through want ol intelligence from family and friends at home. But during the fall, winter and spring there is frequent communication between St. Croix and New York. Many of the regulr traders have very good accommodations lor passengers, and the commanders assiduously provide for the health and comfort of all on board. During a residence at St. Croix one may hear very often from his friends and business. This þÿ frequency of intelligence is exhilarating to the spirits, and is ol no trilling advantage to the health of a feeble invalid. At St. Croix are good boarding houses. þÿ At the other islands, which wc v isited, there were no houses where tut invalid could be made comfortable. Even at Bardadoes the accommodations were very inferior, and the charges extravagantly high. The concourse

ol visiters at St Croix has led to the establishment of several boarding houses, where invalids receive the utmost kindness and attention, and where the charges areas low as the price of the common articles of food will allow. þÿ Miss Briggs particularly, by her unwearied cllorts to promote the comforts of the sick, and to gratify the wishes of all her guests

may be recommended to all who visit the island St. Croix is farther recommended by the pleasant American society, usually congregated there in the winter season. At almost any other island the invalid would have little society, and the tendency to gloom and low spirits, induced by disease, would be agravated bv the loneliness of his situation, and thereby fiis disorder lie increased. But at St. Croix there usually gather in the winter a large number of gentlemen and ladies from America, a very few of whom are reduced low by disease. The greater part of them are persons in delicate health, but abundantly able to walk, visit and ride, and a considerable proportion of the whole number are in perfect health, having come to attend on tfieir enfeebled relatives and friends. Thrown to gether, in a small village, at a distance from their own country, and without regular business. they usually mingle together without ceremony, and by social intercourse, walks and drives, the time is agreeably filled up, which would otherwise be loaded with intolerable ennui. The invalid should remember that the climate alone will not benefit his health. II, during his þÿwinter ssojourn in the balmiest atmosphere, his mind is harrassed with anxiety tor letters from home, or the state ol the roads prevents constant and easy exercise in the carriage or on horseback, or if his accommodations are bad, or if Iiis spijits are depressed for want of society, he will derive little advantage to his health. He must have socie-

t v, exercise, proper food and accommodations, and medicine lor the mind, or a VV est inuia sun will only wither his strength, and send him home more debtlitated than when he left. Now all these auxiliaries to the climate can not be found except in St. Croix. Neither let the invalid expect too much from ilia climate, while he disregards the laws of the animal economy. Some patients are sent to St. Croix, reduced so low by pulmonary complaints that a miracle alone can save them. They die, as a matter of course, and then their friends complain that the benefits of a tinid climate have been exnggera ted, because it has not restored the dead to life. Other invalids, after their arrival here, neglect exercise, eat heartily, lounge away the winter in idleness and ennui, and then blame the climate, because the spring finds them dabilitated by the heat, and still labor ing under comsumption and derangement ol the digestive organs. It should he remem bored that a mild climate is hut one of the means of restoration ; that careful attention to diet is just as necessary in the West Indies as in America : that exercise, in all pulmonary complaints, is essential to recovery ; and that this balmy atmosphere is principally useful by enabling the patient to ride, and al most to live, in the open air. The large number of invalids who spend the winter in St. Croix, mav lie divided into three classes. One class consisted of those who left the United States, with ulceration on their lungs, or with symptoms of incura

hie pulmonary disorder, and in a state ol great debility. These all died, and died pro bably sooner than they would have done had they remained at home. The heat debilitated them, and the disorder rapidly wore them out. The second class consisted of those who left home with alarming, hut not fatal symptoms of pulmonary complaints. But on their ar-

'ival they indulged their appetites with all the luxuries of a West India table, neglected xercise, and speut much time in lounging, deep and laziness These all grew worse. þÿ The third class consisted of those who, with '.omplaints and symptoms like those of the second class þÿ as occasional expectoration of lood, and cough þÿ yet obeyed the laws of hvsiology. They exercised freely þÿ as much is their strength would allow þÿ were reasonibly attentive to their diet, read and visited nough to keep their minds cheerful. These dl grew better. These facts evidently show vhat advice should be given to one who may be considering the expediency of a winter in he West Indies The influence of a West India climate has iteen tried of late years, on the bronchitis. þÿ þÿI be writer of these sketches was himself afdicted with the disorder, and for several successive winters had been troubled with a seere cough occasioned by this inflammation n the throat. The cough ceased immediatev after entering the warm latitudes, and did iot appear in the slightest degree during the vinter But the inflammation in the throat was not removed. The results of his own experience therefore would lead the writer to ioubt whether bronchial affections, unattend- 'd with cough, would be relieved by removal to a warmer climate. But if the irritation in he throat does occasion cough, the balmy air >f St. Croix acts with delightful and almost magical power on the disceased organ. One so afflicted will tie richly rewarded for the

Tub Great Fire in Wilmington. þÿ Very sorry are we to find the catastrophe at Wil" mington, to which we very distrustingly referred yesterday morning, fully confirmed by the southern papers received during the day. The extra from the paper published at that place gives the melancholy details as follows : From the Wilmington Advertiser þÿ Extra, January 17. With a heavy heart we sit down to the task of making a brief record of one of the most disastrous fires, with which our devoted town has ever been visited. At about 2 o'clock this morning the alarm sounded and proved to proceed from the store occupied bv John Dawson, at the North East coiner o' the Court House. The court house itself was soon on fire, as were also me buildings adjoining Mr. Dawson's The flames progressed thence, with terrific fury, in an easterly and northerly direction of the square in which the lire originated, and in a few minutes caught the buildings across Front street, in a westerly direction. The progress of the fire was then in every direction from a common centre. South, however, nothing was bum1 but the court house. In other directions indicated, no barriers could be interposed until the two squares immediately N. W and N- E. of the court house weret ntirelv destroyed, with the exception of the Hank of Cape Fear, and two small houses next north of it. on the former square, and three brick buildings on F. W. angle of the latter. The whole number of buildings destroyed is about one hundred and fiftv, including the offices of the Vd-

vertiser and Chronicle, the Custom House, and the Clarendon and Kenton's Hotel. The following is a list of sufferers, as accurate as it can be made amidst the confusiou of the moment. The Press, and a considerable portion of the materials were saved fioin the Advertiser office, and with them this slip is printed, after the delay consequent upon a hasiv removal of the contents of printing office. a þÿ From the Chronicle office, nothing was saved but the account books. A great deal of goods and furniture were gotton out of the houses and stores, although the loss of proparty of these kinds is immense. Many of the buildings on these two squares were among the most valuable in town, and on these two was done probably three fourths of the business of the place. We have heard no critical estimates of the aggregate loss, but arc inclined to think it will sum up to nearly five hundred thousand dollars. Wiiat portion is insured, is unascertained.

A sloop then hove in sight, and to make them observe me 1 waved my hat. 1 was pretty much chilled through. It was the sloop Merchant, Capt Meeker, who deserves every praise for his conduct.
